To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Higgs boson is produced in proton-nucleus (pA) collisions via gluon-gluonsplitting in the kT factorization framework and the TMD factorisation framework.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of Higgs boson pro-duction in high energy proton nucleus collisions.
the production of a Higgs boson in high energy proton–nucleus collisions.
the study of the Higgs boson in the context of the LHC.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Higgs production in high energy pA collisions is a process where the TMD formalism is applicable, if the gluon distribution function h ⊥g 1 (x, k ⊥) is known, which is not the case at present.
in proton-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions at LHC energies the Higgs boson is produced in a dense medium.
the k t formalism is applicable to the description of Higgs production in proton-nucleus collisons at midrapidity if the gluon distribution function is not too large.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CGC model is able to explain the data for Higgs boson productions in high energy pp collisions and it is also able to predict Higgs bosonproduction rates in high energy proton- nucleus collisions.
the naive k t-factorization framework for the calculation of Higgs production in pA collisions is valid for the dilute regime.
we have shown that the k t -formalism for Higgs-production breaks down in dense media.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the k t formalism for HIGGS production in pA collisions is not valid for dense media and the TMD factorisation is needed.
in the context of high energy proton-nuclear collisions, where the gluon density is large, the k ⊥-factorization approach for Higgs production is not valid.
the k t -factorization formalism for gluon-gluondistribution functions is not applicable to dense systems, and one needs to resort to the TMD factori-zation approach.
